claims.text: Single-phase fcc FeCoNi has high saturation magnetization and coercivity below approximately 100 Oe.
A lower-temperature anneal or modified cooling schedule combined with minor Co-to-Cr substitution can trigger secondary-phase precipitation in an FeCoNi-based alloy.
Composition and annealing temperature control the length scale of secondary-phase decomposition.
The proposed treatment can produce nanoscale B2- or BCC-type particles within an fcc FeCoNi-based matrix.
The secondary-phase particles can remain coherently embedded in the fcc matrix.
A slight Cr substitution can preserve high saturation magnetization.
The structural mediator is a population of nanoscale precipitates or domain-wall pinning centers in the original fcc matrix.
The secondary phase may be B2, BCC, or antiferromagnetic.
Secondary-phase precipitates hinder magnetic domain-wall motion by acting as pinning sites.
Controlled precipitation creates local magnetic inhomogeneities that raise the energy barrier for domain-wall motion.
Hindering domain-wall motion will increase the coercive field.
Co-to-Cr substitution and associated phase decomposition can increase coercivity.
The modified FeCoNi-based alloy will have coercivity significantly above the baseline of less than or approximately 100 Oe.
The coercivity increase can be obtained while retaining reasonably high saturation magnetization.
The magnitude of the coercivity change depends on the volume fraction and distribution of the secondary phase.
Excessive Cr addition may reduce saturation magnetization.
The intervention is restricted to a narrow composition and processing window near FeCoNi that avoids excessive secondary-phase formation.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis expects slight Cr substitution to preserve reasonably high saturation magnetization, whereas the cited evidence reports a substantial reduction in saturation magnetization when Co is replaced by Cr in the studied Al-containing alloy.
